[TODAY] One light-day away: 16 billion miles. 🚀

Today, Nov 18, NASA's Voyager 1 passes more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km) from Earth. That distance is one light-day: light, or a radio command, sent from Earth now needs 24 hours to reach it. No other human-made object has traveled that far.

Voyager 1 launched in 1977, timed to a planetary alignment that comes around once every 176 years. It entered interstellar space in 2012.

Save this if you want to remember how big space really is.

[EMERGING] One infusion cut blood fats 63% on average.

Very high triglycerides, a type of blood fat, raise the risk of heart disease and pancreatitis. In a small Cleveland Clinic trial, 10 adults received one infusion of CTX310, a CRISPR gene-editing treatment that turns off a liver gene that pushes triglycerides up.

Thirty days later, their triglycerides had dropped 63% on average, up to 85% in one case. No serious treatment-related side effects were seen.

Reality check: early results, only 30 days, funded by the company CRISPR Therapeutics. How long it lasts is unknown. This is research news, not medical advice.

[TODAY] A star that erupts every 113 days. 💫

AT 2016blu is a giant star, at least 33 times the Sun's mass, in a galaxy about 30 million light-years away. Since 2012 it has flared at least 27 times, roughly every 113 days. It survived each one. Astronomers call it a supernova impostor.

NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory found the likely cause: a hidden partner, either a black hole or a neutron star, that pulls material from the star on each 113-day orbit. In March 2026 its X-rays were at least 100 times brighter than in 2001-2002.

Reality check: the partner has not been seen directly; this is the team's best explanation.

Black hole or neutron star? Tell us below.

[EMERGING] Who checks a quantum machine's homework?

As quantum simulators grow, ordinary computers can no longer check their answers. A team from the Technical University of Munich and the University of Innsbruck found a way: measure how the machine actually behaves, noise included, rebuild a model of it, then attach error margins to every result. They tested it on 10 trapped ions, which a classical computer can still verify, then on a chain of 51.

Reality check: this is a special-purpose quantum simulator, not a general quantum computer. Two-dimensional systems are the next challenge.

Would you trust an answer you can't check? Tell us below.

[IMAGINE] 1.7 million new satellites are now proposed. 🛰️

What is real: a study by the European Southern Observatory, accepted in Astronomy & Astrophysics, counts proposals for over 1.7 million new satellites. Its simulations show dozens of trails in a single telescope image. A November industry analysis (not peer-reviewed) estimates about 710 already cross a typical town's sky at any moment.

Reality check: these are models of plans not yet launched.

The speculation: what if the next generation grows up under a sky with more satellites than stars?
